summary: Defines the LDAP IntermediateResponse message, a general way to define operations with one request and several responses. It leaves existing LDAP operations unchanged. It updates RFC 2251 and was replaced by RFC 4510 and RFC 4511.

eli5.summary: Sometimes you ask a question and the answer arrives in pieces. This adds a way for a directory to send progress notes before the final answer.

questions: ldap multiple responses to one request
when do you use intermediate response
how is intermediate response different from extended response
subtitle: Progress updates for operations that unfold in stages.

tldr.problem: Most LDAP operations follow a request-then-response pattern, but some tasks (like deleting a subtree or synchronizing data) benefit from intermediate progress updates before the final result.
tldr.mechanism: IntermediateResponse is a new LDAP message type that an extended operation or control can use to send progress information back to the client before the final response arrives.
tldr.outcome: Clients waiting for a long operation can now get status updates as the server works, and do not have to wait for the final result to receive continuation references or other partial information.

today: RFC 3771 was obsoleted by RFC 4510 and RFC 4511, which are the newer consolidated LDAP specifications. IntermediateResponse remains a core part of modern LDAP.

sections.title: Single-Request, Multiple-Response Operations
sections.content:
LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) is designed as a request-response system: you ask the server for something, and it sends back one final answer. But some operations do not fit neatly into that mold.

For example, when you delete a directory subtree, the server finds references to other servers that might hold related data (subordinate knowledge information). It could wait until the entire deletion is done, then list all the references; but it is more efficient to send each reference back as the server finds it. The client can then act on each reference immediately, instead of waiting.

Similarly, an operation that happens in stages—like creating a new replica—might want to send a status message at each stage, so the client knows the work is progressing.
sections.eli5: Imagine telling someone to deliver mail to 100 houses. They could come back to you after visiting all 100 with the total count, or they could stop by every 10 houses to tell you where they are.

sections.title: The IntermediateResponse Message
sections.content:
RFC 3771 defines a new LDAP message type called IntermediateResponse (message type 25) that carries intermediate result information. It is a simple structure: an optional responseName (an identifier for the type of response) and optional responseValue (the data).

IntermediateResponse messages are not sent automatically. The client must explicitly request them by using an extended operation or a request control that calls for their return. Once requested, the server can send zero or more IntermediateResponse messages followed by the final result.
sections.eli5: IntermediateResponse is a way for the server to send progress notes before the final answer. You only get them if you ask for them.

sections.title: Two Ways to Use IntermediateResponse
sections.content:
With extended operations: An ExtendedRequest message can solicit zero or more IntermediateResponse messages before the final ExtendedResponse arrives. When multiple kinds of intermediate responses are defined, the extended operation must document a way for the client to tell them apart (usually by giving each type a different responseName).

With controls: A control attached to any LDAP operation can specify that IntermediateResponse messages be returned. Here, all IntermediateResponse messages must include a responseName so the client can identify which control generated each one, even if multiple controls are present in the same request.
sections.eli5: IntermediateResponse works with two LDAP features. With extended operations, it is part of a new feature. With controls, it enhances an existing operation.

sections.title: Why Not Reuse ExtendedResponse?
sections.content:
ExtendedResponse already exists in LDAP and is used for returning results of extended operations and unsolicited notifications. Why define a new message type?

The reason is compatibility and implementation simplicity. Existing LDAP APIs and implementations treat ExtendedResponse as the final result message. Reusing it for intermediate results would require redesigning APIs and would likely break existing code. A separate message type is cleaner to implement and less likely to cause interoperability problems.
sections.eli5: LDAP already had a message for final answers. Adding intermediate messages as a new type is simpler than reusing the old one.

sections.title: No New Security Issues
sections.content:
IntermediateResponse does not introduce new security concerns beyond those of LDAP itself. The mechanism is a protocol extension that carries the same data that operations would eventually send anyway; it just sends parts of it earlier.

Each extended operation or control that uses IntermediateResponse must document its own security considerations, such as what information is revealed in intermediate messages and when.
sections.eli5: IntermediateResponse is not less secure than LDAP; it just breaks up the conversation into more pieces.
